before.q: A rational person takes an action when:
options: Marginal benefit is greater than marginal cost
Total cost is always higher than total benefit
There is no opportunity cost
The action is popular
before.feedback: Marginal reasoning compares the extra benefit to the extra cost.

after.q: A delivery service considers accepting one more order. The order adds $28 in revenue and $19 in delivery cost. What should it do?
options: Accept because the added benefit exceeds the added cost
Reject because any additional cost makes the order harmful
Accept only if total daily revenue exceeds total daily cost
Reject unless average delivery cost falls after the order
after.commonError: Using totals or averages instead of the next order’s values.
after.feedback: The additional order adds $9 in net benefit.

before.q: You buy one more study guide because the extra benefit exceeds the extra cost. What kind of reasoning is this?
options: Marginal reasoning
Tax incidence
Circular-flow reasoning
Price ceiling analysis
before.feedback: The phrase one more points to marginal reasoning.

after.q: A student asks whether one more study hour is worthwhile by comparing its expected grade improvement with the fatigue it creates. What reasoning is being used?
options: Marginal reasoning about one additional hour
Average reasoning about all study hours combined
Sunk-cost reasoning about time already spent
Total-benefit reasoning without considering added cost
after.commonError: Missing the one-more-unit focus of marginal analysis.
after.feedback: The question compares the benefit and cost created by one additional hour.

before.q: A decision should be expanded by one more unit when:
options: A large amount has already been spent under the stated conditions.
Total benefit is positive in the situation described.
Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
Average benefit exceeds average cost for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Using averages, totals, or sunk costs instead of marginal values.
before.feedback: The marginal rule compares the added benefit with the added cost of the next unit.

after.q: A food truck can serve one more customer for $11 in added revenue and $8 in added food and labor cost. Which choice follows the marginal rule?
options: Serve the customer because marginal benefit covers marginal cost
Stop because the customer creates a positive cost
Serve only if average revenue for the day rises
Stop unless earlier setup expenses have been recovered
after.commonError: Rejecting any costly unit or using averages and sunk costs.
after.feedback: The next customer adds $3 in net benefit, so service should continue.

options: A cost that has already been paid.
The additional benefit from one more unit.
The average benefit per unit.
The total benefit from all units.
before.commonError: Confusing marginal with total or average.
before.feedback: Marginal benefit is the change in total benefit from one additional unit.

after.q: A clinic adds one appointment and total patient benefit rises from 40 to 47 points. What is the marginal benefit of that appointment?
options: 7 benefit points
47 total benefit points
40 prior benefit points
43.5 average benefit points
after.commonError: Reporting the new total or an average instead of the change.
after.feedback: Marginal benefit is the change in total benefit: 47 minus 40.

before.q: Which statement best distinguishes marginal cost from average cost?
options: Average cost measures only fixed cost as the relevant economic conclusion.
Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit; average cost is total cost per unit.
The two measures are identical at every output as the relevant economic conclusion.
Marginal cost is always lower than average cost for the decision being evaluated.
before.commonError: Treating marginal and average values as interchangeable.
before.feedback: Marginal and average costs answer different questions.

after.q: A factory’s average cost is $14, while producing unit 101 raises total cost from $1,400 to $1,418. Which cost is relevant to the unit-101 decision?
options: The $18 marginal cost of unit 101
The $14 average cost of existing output
The $1,418 total cost after production
The $1,400 cost already incurred
after.commonError: Using average or total cost instead of the added cost.
after.feedback: Unit 101 changes total cost by $18; that increment is its marginal cost.

before.q: A company already spent $80,000 developing software. It can spend $15,000 more to launch and expects $20,000 in revenue. What is the best marginal decision?
options: Launch because the additional benefit exceeds the additional cost by $5,000
Do not launch because total cost is $95,000
Launch only if revenue covers the sunk $80,000
Do not launch because sunk costs always matter most
before.feedback: The $80,000 is sunk. The launch decision compares the extra $15,000 cost to the extra $20,000 revenue.

after.q: A vaccine trial can enroll one more site. The site has a 60% chance of producing evidence worth $50,000 and costs $24,000 to operate. Ignoring other effects, what does expected marginal analysis recommend?
options: Enroll because expected marginal benefit is $30,000, above cost
Reject because the full $50,000 benefit is uncertain
Enroll only if earlier research spending is recovered
Reject because the $24,000 cost raises total trial spending
after.commonError: Ignoring probability or including sunk research spending.
after.feedback: Expected added benefit is 0.60 × $50,000 = $30,000, which exceeds $24,000.

before.q: A manager has already spent $40,000 developing a product. Finishing it costs $12,000 more and is expected to bring in $18,000. What should the manager do using marginal reasoning?
options: Finish it because the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost
Cancel it because total cost is $52,000
Finish it because sunk costs should determine the choice
Cancel it because marginal cost is always bad
before.feedback: The $40,000 is sunk. The relevant comparison is $18,000 in added benefit versus $12,000 in added cost.

after.q: A cyber-security team can run one more audit. It costs 90 staff-hours and is expected to prevent 120 hours of incident response, but the audit also displaces training worth 20 hours. What is the net marginal effect?
options: A gain of 10 staff-hours
A gain of 30 staff-hours
A loss of 70 staff-hours
A gain of 210 staff-hours
after.commonError: Ignoring the displaced alternative or adding costs and benefits.
after.feedback: Net marginal effect is 120 minus 90 direct hours minus 20 displaced training hours.

before.q: The Signal Breaker says: 'Do not ask what was already spent. Ask what changes next.' What kind of reasoning is this?
options: Marginal reasoning
GDP accounting
Tax incidence
Price floor analysis
before.feedback: Marginal reasoning compares the extra benefit and extra cost of the next action.

after.q: A bookstore considers staying open one more hour. The hour adds $240 in sales margin and $170 in staffing and utility cost. Which comparison matters?
options: The $240 added benefit versus the $170 added cost
Total yearly sales versus total yearly operating and staffing cost
Average hourly sales versus the original opening expense
Past rent payments versus today’s entire revenue
after.commonError: Using total, average, or sunk values instead of next-hour changes.
after.feedback: Marginal analysis isolates what changes during the additional hour.

before.q: A trader gains 30 tokens from one more deal, but the deal costs 18 tokens to complete. What should the trader do?
options: Take the deal because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost
Reject the deal because any cost is bad
Take the deal only if there is no opportunity cost
Reject the deal because total cost matters most
before.feedback: The marginal benefit is 30 and the marginal cost is 18, so the net gain is positive.

after.q: A grocer can stock one more crate. Expected sales margin is $45, spoilage risk costs $12, and shelf labor costs $18. What should the grocer do?
options: Stock it because the $45 benefit exceeds the $30 added cost
Reject it because spoilage risk makes total benefit uncertain
Stock it only if the store’s average profit increases
Reject it because both cost items must be added to revenue
after.commonError: Ignoring a cost component or adding benefit and cost.
after.feedback: Marginal cost is $30, leaving $15 in net marginal benefit.

before.q: “Do not ask what was already spent. Ask what changes next.” What principle does this describe?
options: Marginal reasoning
Tax incidence
A price ceiling
Circular flow
before.feedback: Marginal reasoning compares the extra benefit and extra cost of the next action.

after.q: A nurse can make one more follow-up call. The expected patient benefit is 12 points and the fatigue cost is 8 points. What should the nurse do?
options: Make the call because its marginal benefit exceeds its marginal cost
Skip the call because fatigue creates any positive cost
Make the call only if average benefit per call rises
Skip the call unless total benefit exceeds all past costs
after.commonError: Reversing the MB-MC rule or using averages and totals.
after.feedback: The next call adds 4 points of net benefit.

options: Average benefit and average cost only.
Total benefit and total cost only.
The added benefit and added cost of the next unit.
Past benefit and past cost.
before.commonError: Confusing marginal with total or average analysis.
before.feedback: The marginal question is what changes if one more unit is chosen.

after.q: A school considers one more tutoring session. Total benefit would rise from 72 to 80 points and total cost from 48 to 54 points. Which values should be compared?
options: Marginal benefit 8 and marginal cost 6
Total benefit 80 and total cost 54
Average benefit 76 and average cost 51
Prior benefit 72 and prior cost 48
after.commonError: Comparing totals or averages instead of their changes.
after.feedback: The additional session adds 8 benefit points and 6 cost points.

before.q: MB values are 30, 22, 14, 8 and MC values are 10, 16, 15, 12. What quantity is optimal?
options: One unit.
Four units.
Three units.
Two units.
before.commonError: Continuing past the point where MC exceeds MB.
before.feedback: The first two units add net benefit; the third does not.

after.q: MB values for units 1 through 4 are 30, 22, 14, and 8; MC values are 10, 16, 15, and 12. Which production plan is optimal?
options: Produce only unit 1
Produce all four units
Produce the first three units
Produce the first two units
after.commonError: Continuing after marginal cost first exceeds marginal benefit.
after.feedback: Units 1 and 2 add net benefit; unit 3 would reduce it.

before.q: A warehouse has packed 900 orders. Packing the next 100 orders costs $1,600 in overtime and avoids $2,100 in late-delivery penalties. What should it do?
options: Stop because total overtime is already high
Pack the next 100 because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost
Pack them only if average cost falls
Stop because penalties are not revenue
before.feedback: The relevant comparison is the $2,100 avoided penalty versus the $1,600 added cost.

after.q: A warehouse has packed 900 orders. Packing the next 100 costs $1,600 in overtime and avoids $2,100 in late-delivery penalties. What should it do?
options: Pack them because the avoided penalty exceeds added overtime cost
Stop because total overtime is already high
Pack them only if average cost falls
Stop because avoided penalties are not marginal benefits
after.commonError: Ignoring avoided costs or relying on total and average values.
after.feedback: The next 100 orders create $500 in net marginal benefit.

before.q: A software firm has spent $2 million on a product. One final update costs $90,000 and is expected to generate $70,000 in additional revenue. What is the marginal decision?
options: Release because the total investment is too large to abandon
Release because average revenue may rise
Do not release because the added cost exceeds the added benefit
Do not release because all past spending was wasteful
before.feedback: Past spending is sunk. The final update has a $90,000 marginal cost and only a $70,000 marginal benefit.

after.q: A software firm has spent $2 million on a product. One final update costs $90,000 and is expected to generate $70,000 in additional revenue. What is the marginal decision?
options: Do not release because added cost exceeds added benefit
Release because the total investment is large
Release because average revenue may rise
Do not release because all past spending was wasteful
after.commonError: Letting sunk investment override a negative next increment.
after.feedback: Past spending is sunk; the final update loses $20,000 at the margin.

before.q: A transit system can add buses one at a time. The next three buses have marginal benefits of $140k, $105k, and $78k; each has a marginal cost of $100k. How many should be added?
options: One
Two
Three
Zero
before.feedback: Add buses while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost. The first two qualify; the third does not.

after.q: A transit system can add buses one at a time. The next three buses have marginal benefits of $140k, $105k, and $78k; each costs $100k. How many should be added?
options: Two
One
Three
Zero
after.commonError: Stopping early or continuing after MB falls below MC.
after.feedback: The first two buses pass the marginal test; the third does not.

before.q: An extra tutoring session is expected to improve performance by 7 points and creates 4 points of fatigue cost. What is the net marginal benefit?
options: 3 points.
4 points.
11 points.
7 points.
before.commonError: Failing to subtract marginal cost from marginal benefit.

after.q: Scarcity limits a community’s emergency crews. How does marginal analysis help decide whether to assign one more crew-hour to inspections?
options: Compare the added inspection benefit with the best use of that crew-hour forgone
Add the value of every program the community cannot fund
Use total inspection benefit without considering the next hour’s cost
Treat all prior emergency spending as the next hour’s marginal cost
after.commonError: Failing to connect scarce-resource tradeoffs to the next increment.
after.feedback: Scarcity makes the crew-hour costly; marginal analysis tests whether its added inspection benefit covers that cost.

before.q: A company has spent heavily on a failing product. Future revenue is $40,000 and future completion cost is $55,000. What should it do?
options: Continue because much has already been spent.
Stop development unless another future benefit exists.
Continue because revenue is positive.
Ignore future cost because the project is nearly complete.
before.commonError: Failing to transfer sunk-cost reasoning to a business case.
before.feedback: Past spending is irrelevant; the future cost exceeds the future benefit.

after.q: A worker could earn $25 during one more study hour. How does opportunity cost enter the marginal study decision?
options: The forgone $25 is part of the marginal cost of that hour
The $25 is a sunk cost because work has not occurred
All lifetime wages become the marginal cost of studying
Opportunity cost matters only for the first study hour
after.commonError: Ignoring the best alternative use of the next increment.
after.feedback: The next hour’s opportunity cost belongs in its marginal cost.

after.q: A student considers studying one more hour. Expected exam benefit is 6 points and fatigue cost is 4 points. What should the student do?
options: Study because the added benefit exceeds the added cost
Stop because any fatigue makes studying harmful
Study only if average grades rise
Stop unless prior study time is recovered
after.commonError: Rejecting a positive-net increment or using averages and sunk effort.
after.feedback: The extra hour adds 2 points of net benefit.

after.q: A restaurant can serve one more table for $70 in added revenue and $52 in added cost. Which amount is net marginal benefit?
after.commonError: Adding benefit and cost or reporting only one side.
after.feedback: Net marginal benefit is $70 minus $52.

after.q: A store has already paid monthly rent. When deciding whether to stay open one more hour, how should that rent be treated?
options: As a sunk cost that does not change with the hour
As the marginal cost of every extra hour
As the marginal benefit of added sales
As an avoidable cost only if sales are low
after.commonError: Assigning a fixed past payment to the next-hour decision.
after.feedback: Only costs that change with the additional hour are marginal.

after.q: A clinic can treat one more patient. Which question is marginal?
options: What added benefit and added cost will this patient create?
What have all patients cost since the clinic opened?
What is average benefit across all patients?
How large was the clinic’s original construction budget?
after.commonError: Substituting total, average, or historical values for the next increment.
after.feedback: Marginal analysis asks what changes because of one additional patient.

after.q: Total benefit rises from $140 to $158 when a fifth unit is added, while total cost rises from $92 to $107. What is the fifth unit’s net marginal benefit?
after.commonError: Comparing totals or adding the two marginal changes.
after.feedback: MB is $18 and MC is $15, so net marginal benefit is $3.

after.q: A warehouse’s average handling cost is $9 per box, but the next box costs $13 to handle and creates $15 in margin. What should it do?
options: Handle it because $15 exceeds the $13 marginal cost
Reject it because marginal cost exceeds average cost
Handle it only if average cost falls below $9
Reject it because total handling cost rises
after.commonError: Using average cost instead of the next box’s cost.
after.feedback: The box adds $2 in profit even though its marginal cost exceeds average cost.

after.q: A firm can run up to four ads. Their marginal benefits are $90, $70, $45, and $20; each ad costs $50. How many ads should run?
options: Two ads
One ad
Three ads
Four ads
after.commonError: Stopping early or continuing after MB falls below MC.
after.feedback: Only the first two ads have marginal benefit at least $50.

after.q: A project has an unrecoverable $8,000 design cost. Finishing costs $3,000 and yields $4,200; cancellation costs $400. Which comparison is relevant?
options: Finish for a $1,200 future gain versus paying $400 to cancel
Compare the full $11,000 spending with $4,200 revenue
Finish only to recover the $8,000 design cost
Cancel because any remaining cost is harmful
after.commonError: Including sunk design cost or ignoring the cancellation alternative.
after.feedback: The future choices are a $1,200 net gain from finishing or a $400 cancellation cost.

after.q: A sixth quality inspection lowers expected defect losses by $260 and costs $210 in labor. What is the correct next-step decision?
options: Perform it because avoided loss is a marginal benefit above cost
Skip it because inspection creates a positive labor cost
Perform it only if total defect losses become zero
Skip it unless average inspection cost falls
after.commonError: Ignoring avoided cost as benefit or using totals and averages.
after.feedback: The inspection creates $50 in net marginal benefit.

after.q: One more worker adds $620 in output but requires $480 in wages and $90 in added equipment use. What is the worker’s net marginal contribution?
after.commonError: Omitting a cost component or reporting gross output.
after.feedback: $620 minus $480 minus $90 equals $50.

after.q: An airline can sell one more seat for $240. Added catering and handling cost $35, and accepting the passenger displaces cargo margin of $170. What is net marginal benefit?
after.commonError: Ignoring opportunity cost or adding benefit and costs.
after.feedback: Net benefit is $240 minus $35 direct cost minus $170 forgone cargo margin.

after.q: A city considers a third congestion-reduction measure. Driver time savings are $1.4 million, implementation costs $900,000, and added neighborhood noise costs $600,000. What should it do?
options: Reject because marginal social cost is $1.5 million
Adopt because private implementation cost is below benefit
Adopt because total time savings remain positive
Reject only if average program cost rises
after.commonError: Ignoring an external marginal cost.
after.feedback: Implementation plus noise costs exceed the next measure’s benefit.

after.q: Total revenue at 200 units is $18,000 and at 201 units is $18,075. Total cost rises from $14,400 to $14,482. Should unit 201 be produced?
options: No, because marginal revenue $75 is below marginal cost $82
Yes, because total revenue remains above total cost
Yes, because average profit is positive
No, because total cost rises when the unit is produced
after.commonError: Using positive total or average profit instead of the next unit.
after.feedback: Unit 201 reduces profit by $7.

after.q: A hospital can add a night shift. Expected benefit is $31,000; added payroll is $22,000; and using the nurses displaces training worth $11,000. Which decision is best?
options: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $33,000
Add it because payroll alone is below benefit
Add it because total hospital benefit is large
Do not add it because any displaced activity is sunk
after.commonError: Ignoring the next-best alternative use of staff time.
after.feedback: Payroll plus forgone training exceeds the shift’s expected benefit.

after.q: A research grant has spent $2 million. Another experiment costs $180,000 and has a 40% chance of producing evidence worth $600,000. Ignoring other outcomes, should it run?
options: Run because expected marginal benefit is $240,000
Stop because the $600,000 benefit is uncertain
Run only to justify the $2 million already spent
Stop because total spending would rise
after.commonError: Ignoring probability or including sunk grant spending.
after.feedback: Expected added benefit exceeds the $180,000 experiment cost.

after.q: A retailer’s first three added inventory batches have net marginal benefits of $6,000, $2,000, and -$1,500. A fourth would have +$500 only if the third is purchased. What is the best discrete choice?
options: Buy two batches
Buy four batches
Buy three batches
Buy one batch
after.commonError: Crossing a negative increment to reach a smaller later positive one.
after.feedback: Buying batches three and four together would reduce net benefit by $1,000.

after.q: A flood barrier segment has a 30% chance of preventing $10 million in damage, costs $2.4 million, and creates $900,000 in expected habitat loss. What does social marginal analysis recommend?
options: Do not build because expected benefit is $3 million and social cost is $3.3 million
Build because expected damage avoided exceeds construction cost
Build because the possible gross benefit is $10 million
Do not build because uncertain benefits should count as zero
after.commonError: Ignoring probability or external marginal cost.
after.feedback: Expected benefit is below construction plus habitat cost.

after.q: A platform can add one feature now for $80,000. It yields $95,000 in direct benefit but delays a security upgrade worth $25,000. What is the feature’s net marginal effect?
after.commonError: Ignoring the displaced incremental alternative.
after.feedback: $95,000 minus $80,000 direct cost minus $25,000 opportunity cost equals -$10,000.

after.q: A hospital considers a fifth treatment slot. Expected health benefit is 70 points, direct cost is 45 points, and the slot displaces emergency readiness worth 30 points. What is the decision?
options: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is 75 points
Add it because direct cost is below health benefit
Add it because total hospital benefit remains high
Do not add it because displaced readiness is sunk
after.commonError: Ignoring the best alternative use of the next slot.
after.feedback: Direct and opportunity costs exceed the added treatment benefit.

after.q: An airline’s next flight frequency adds $80,000 in revenue, $54,000 in operating cost, and $18,000 in expected delay costs imposed on other flights. What is net marginal benefit?
after.commonError: Ignoring congestion cost or adding benefit and costs.

after.q: A software team’s next sprint has a 50% chance of creating $180,000 in value and costs $70,000. It also delays maintenance worth $25,000. What should it do?
options: Do not run it because expected benefit $90,000 is below relevant cost $95,000
Run it because possible benefit is $180,000
Run it because sprint cost alone is below expected benefit
Do not run it because uncertainty makes expected benefit zero
after.commonError: Ignoring probability or displaced maintenance.
after.feedback: Expected benefit is $90,000; direct plus opportunity cost is $95,000.

after.q: A city can add four road-maintenance zones. Marginal benefits are 14, 11, 8, and 5; marginal costs are 6, 8, 9, and 10. How many zones should be added?
options: Two zones
One zone
Three zones
Four zones
after.commonError: Continuing after MC exceeds MB or stopping too soon.
after.feedback: The first two zones add net benefit; the third does not.

after.q: A pollution rule’s next reduction step yields $4.8 million in health benefit, costs firms $3.6 million, and prevents recreation worth $1.5 million. What is the social marginal choice?
options: Do not require it because social marginal cost is $5.1 million
Require it because compliance cost alone is below benefit
Require it because total prior health benefits are large
Do not require it because all environmental policy is costly
after.commonError: Ignoring a relevant external or opportunity cost.
after.feedback: The next step’s combined social costs exceed its benefit.

after.q: A factory’s total defect-reduction benefit rises from $900,000 to $970,000 with a sixth inspection station. Total cost rises from $610,000 to $688,000. Should it add the station?
options: No, because MB is $70,000 and MC is $78,000
Yes, because total benefit exceeds total cost
Yes, because average benefit remains positive
No, because total cost would increase
after.commonError: Using favorable totals instead of unfavorable margins.
after.feedback: The sixth station reduces net benefit by $8,000.

after.q: A police department considers one more patrol. Crime reduction is valued at $120,000, added payroll is $75,000, and the officers would forgo training worth $38,000. What is net marginal benefit?
after.commonError: Ignoring forgone training or adding values.

after.q: A research fund can award grants sequentially. The next grants have expected net marginal benefits of $2.0m, $0.7m, -$0.4m, and $0.6m, but each later grant requires all earlier ones. How many should be awarded?
options: Two grants
Four grants
Three grants
One grant
after.commonError: Crossing a negative required increment to reach a later positive increment.
after.feedback: The third and fourth together reduce net benefit, so stop after two.

after.q: A tutoring program’s average benefit per student is 16 points. The next student adds 9 benefit points and costs 7 points to serve. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Enroll the student because the marginal comparison is favorable
Reject because marginal benefit is below average benefit
Enroll only if average benefit rises above 16
Reject because total program cost rises
after.commonError: Using an average benchmark instead of MB versus MC.
after.feedback: The next student adds 2 points of net benefit.

after.q: A manufacturer has $3 million in fixed plant cost. Unit 501 adds $420 in revenue, $310 in materials, and $85 in overtime. What should it do?
options: Produce because the unit adds $25 in profit
Stop because fixed plant cost is large
Produce only if average total cost falls
Stop because total cost increases by $395
after.commonError: Allocating fixed or total cost to the next-unit rule.
after.feedback: Only the $395 avoidable cost matters for unit 501.

after.q: A utility considers one more conservation rebate. Expected energy savings are $130, rebate administration costs $90, and customer hassle is valued at $45. What is the social decision?
options: Do not offer it because marginal social cost is $135
Offer it because administrative cost is below savings
Offer it because total energy savings remain positive
Do not offer it because rebates are transfers
after.commonError: Ignoring a nonbudget marginal cost.
after.feedback: The next rebate’s social cost exceeds its benefit by $5.

after.q: A marketing campaign has already cost $400,000. One final placement costs $60,000 and has a 75% chance of adding $100,000 in profit. Should it run?
options: Run because expected marginal benefit is $75,000
Stop because the full campaign cost is high
Run only to recover the $400,000 already spent
Stop because the gross benefit is uncertain
after.commonError: Ignoring probability or including sunk campaign spending.
after.feedback: Expected added profit exceeds the placement’s added cost.

after.q: An emergency agency can pre-position one more team. Expected response benefit is $500,000, deployment costs $320,000, and the team’s best alternative assignment is worth $210,000. What should it do?
options: Do not deploy because relevant marginal cost is $530,000
Deploy because direct cost is below expected benefit
Deploy because emergency benefits are not monetary
Do not deploy because prior readiness spending is sunk
after.commonError: Ignoring the alternative assignment of the next team.
after.feedback: Direct plus opportunity cost exceeds expected response benefit.

after.q: A bus route’s total rider benefit at 12 trips is 840 points and at 13 trips is 892. Total operating cost rises from 610 to 655. What is trip 13’s net marginal benefit?
options: 7 points
45 points
52 points
237 points
after.commonError: Comparing totals or reporting one marginal change.
after.feedback: MB is 52 and MC is 45, leaving 7 points.

after.q: A farm’s next fertilizer application raises crop value by $1,100, costs $760, and increases expected water cleanup by $390. Which statement is correct?
options: Do not apply because marginal social cost exceeds benefit by $50
Apply because private marginal profit is $340
Apply because total crop revenue is positive
Do not apply because fertilizer cost is sunk
after.commonError: Using only private marginal cost.
after.feedback: Combined marginal cost is $1,150, above the $1,100 benefit.

after.q: A university pilot has spent $6 million. Extending it costs $900,000 and yields $1.1 million in expected benefit, while ending now requires $250,000 in transition cost. What is best?
options: Extend because its future net gain exceeds the cost of ending
End because total spending is already too high
Extend only to avoid wasting the $6 million
End because transition cost is less than extension cost
after.commonError: Comparing gross future costs or sunk totals instead of future alternatives.
after.feedback: Extending gains $200,000, while ending loses $250,000.

after.q: A city adds park lighting in blocks. Marginal benefits are 100, 82, 61, and 40; private costs are 55 each, but marginal light-pollution costs are 10, 18, 25, and 32. How many blocks should be lit?
options: Two blocks
One block
Three blocks
Four blocks
after.commonError: Ignoring changing external costs or continuing one unit too far.
after.feedback: Social MC is 65, 73, 80, and 87; only the first two pass.

after.q: A nonprofit can deliver one more meal route. Donations attributable to the route are $900, food and fuel cost $620, and volunteer time displaces tutoring worth $310. What is the choice?
options: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $930
Add it because direct cost is below donations
Add it because volunteer time is unpaid
Do not add it because total program costs are high
after.commonError: Treating unpaid resources as zero marginal cost.
after.feedback: Direct plus forgone volunteer value exceeds added donations.

after.q: A maintenance team can inspect another bridge. The inspection costs $70,000 and has a 20% chance of preventing $500,000 in repairs. What is expected net marginal benefit?
after.commonError: Using gross possible savings or ignoring probability.
after.feedback: Expected benefit is $100,000; subtracting $70,000 gives $30,000.

after.q: A data center’s next cooling upgrade saves $140,000 in expected outages, costs $100,000, and uses technicians who could complete security work worth $50,000. What should it do?
options: Do not upgrade because relevant marginal cost is $150,000
Upgrade because outage savings exceed direct cost
Upgrade because technicians are already salaried
Do not upgrade because total cooling spending is high
after.commonError: Ignoring the next-best use of salaried labor.
after.feedback: Direct and opportunity costs exceed the expected outage savings.

after.q: A school intervention’s next class has gross benefit 44 points, delivery cost 30, and teacher fatigue cost 9. A later class would yield gross benefit 50 but requires this class first. What should the school do now?
options: Deliver the next class because its net marginal benefit is 5
Skip to the later class because its gross benefit is higher
Stop because combined cost is positive
Deliver only if average class benefit rises
after.commonError: Skipping a required increment or using gross and average values.
after.feedback: The current required class has positive net marginal benefit.

after.q: A firm’s average profit is positive. The next order adds $180 in revenue and $205 in avoidable cost. What should it do?
options: Reject the order because its marginal contribution is negative
Accept because average profit across all prior orders remains positive
Accept because total revenue will rise
Reject only if fixed cost also rises
after.commonError: Using positive average profit instead of the next order’s margin.
after.feedback: The order reduces profit by $25.

after.q: Total benefit rises from 300 to 336 with one more unit; total cost rises from 210 to 242. What should happen?
options: Add the unit because MB 36 exceeds MC 32
Stop because total cost rises by 32
Add only if average benefit increases
Stop because total cost remains positive
after.commonError: Using totals or treating any added cost as disqualifying.
after.feedback: The next unit adds 4 in net benefit.

after.q: A project has $10 million in sunk spending. Completion costs $3 million, yields $3.4 million, and displaces another project worth $0.6 million. What is the decision?
options: Do not complete because relevant marginal cost is $3.6 million
Complete because future revenue exceeds direct cost
Complete to recover the $10 million
Do not complete because total project cost is high
after.commonError: Ignoring the displaced project or including sunk spending.
after.feedback: Direct plus opportunity cost exceeds future benefit.

after.q: One more factory inspection avoids expected losses of $95,000, costs $62,000, and creates $38,000 in delay costs for customers. What is the social choice?
options: Skip it because marginal social cost is $100,000
Perform it because direct cost is below avoided loss
Perform it because total quality benefit is positive
Skip it because all delay costs are sunk
after.commonError: Ignoring an external marginal cost.
after.feedback: The inspection’s combined added cost exceeds avoided loss.

after.q: A city can add flood sensors. MB values are 90, 72, 50, 31 and MC values are 40, 60, 55, 48. How many should be added?
options: Two
One
Three
Four
after.commonError: Continuing after MC exceeds MB or stopping early.
after.feedback: Only the first two sensors have MB at least MC.

after.q: A project has spent $5 million. Finishing costs $900,000, yields $1.0 million, and cancellation costs $180,000. What is best?
options: Finish because its $100,000 future gain beats the cancellation loss
Cancel because remaining cost is larger than cancellation cost
Finish only to recover the sunk $5 million
Cancel because total spending already exceeds revenue
after.commonError: Comparing gross future costs or sunk totals instead of net alternatives.
after.feedback: Finishing gains $100,000; cancellation loses $180,000.

after.q: A hospital’s next mobile unit yields expected benefit $700,000, costs $520,000, and displaces prevention work worth $210,000. What should it do?
options: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $730,000
Add it because direct cost is below benefit
Add it because prevention work is noncash
Do not add it because total hospital cost is high
after.commonError: Ignoring the forgone use of the next resource increment.
after.feedback: Direct and opportunity cost exceed expected benefit.

after.q: A manufacturer’s next worker adds $1,400 in output, costs $980 in wages, and requires $260 in added equipment. What is net marginal contribution?
after.commonError: Omitting a cost component or reporting gross output.
after.feedback: $1,400 minus $980 minus $260 equals $160.

after.q: A cleanup step yields $500 in benefit, costs $370 privately, and creates $150 in habitat disruption. What is the social decision?
options: Do not take it because social MC is $520
Take it because private MC is below benefit
Take it because total cleanup benefit is positive
Do not take it because habitat costs are sunk
after.commonError: Ignoring external marginal cost.
after.feedback: Combined marginal cost exceeds benefit by $20.

after.q: A test has a 25% chance of avoiding $800,000 in losses and costs $170,000. Ignoring other effects, should it be run?
options: Run because expected marginal benefit is $200,000
Stop because the $800,000 benefit is uncertain
Run only if past testing costs are recovered
Stop because any test cost raises total spending
after.commonError: Ignoring probability or sunk testing expenditure.
after.feedback: Expected benefit exceeds marginal cost by $30,000.

after.q: Total benefit is 50 and average benefit is 10. One more unit raises total benefit to 57. What is marginal benefit?
after.commonError: Reporting total or average benefit instead of the change.
after.feedback: Marginal benefit is 57 minus 50.

after.q: Marginal cost is $12 and marginal benefit is $17. What should happen?
options: Take the next unit because benefit exceeds cost
Stop because the unit has a positive cost
Add $12 and $17 before deciding
Use average cost instead of marginal cost
after.commonError: Reversing the marginal rule or adding MB and MC.
after.feedback: Compare MB with MC; the next unit adds $5 in net benefit.

after.q: Which value is average rather than marginal?
options: Total cost divided by all units produced
The change in cost from one more unit
The benefit added by the next unit
A future cost avoided by stopping now
after.commonError: Treating an average per unit as the next unit’s change.
after.feedback: Average divides a total across units; marginal measures a change.

after.q: A $100 fee is refundable if a project stops today. Is it sunk for today’s decision?
options: No, because stopping can still recover it
Yes, because it was paid in the past
Yes, because every prior payment is sunk
No, because future costs can never matter
after.commonError: Calling a recoverable or avoidable cost sunk.
after.feedback: A cost is sunk only if the current choice cannot recover or avoid it.

after.q: One more sale brings $30 in revenue and requires $22 in added cost. What is net marginal benefit?
after.commonError: Adding benefit and cost or reporting gross revenue.
after.feedback: Net marginal benefit equals $30 minus $22.

after.q: A firm expands output while the revenue from one more unit exceeds the cost of that unit. How does this connect marginal analysis to profit maximization?
options: Each positive marginal contribution raises profit until the next unit turns negative
Profit is maximized whenever total revenue is positive
Fixed cost determines whether every additional unit is produced
Average revenue must exceed total cost for the next unit
after.commonError: Using totals or fixed costs instead of incremental profit.
after.feedback: Profit rises while marginal revenue covers marginal cost.

after.q: A factory’s next unit creates pollution damage not paid by the factory. How does that affect marginal analysis?
options: The external damage belongs in social marginal cost
The damage is sunk because outsiders bear it
Only private production cost can be marginal
External damage matters only after all output is produced
after.commonError: Leaving external incremental harm out of social decisions.
after.feedback: Social marginal analysis counts costs imposed on others.

after.q: A public program considers one additional service. How does marginal analysis implement cost-benefit reasoning?
options: Compare the added social benefit with the added social cost
Compare lifetime total program spending with the current year’s available budget
Add average benefit and average cost together
Continue whenever any participant receives a benefit
after.commonError: Replacing the next increment with totals or averages.
after.feedback: Cost-benefit analysis at the margin asks whether the next increment creates net social benefit.

after.q: A consumer buys another unit while its added satisfaction exceeds the price and other next-unit costs. What connection is being made?
options: Consumer choice can use the same MB-versus-MC rule
Consumer choice depends only on total satisfaction accumulated from every prior purchase
The price becomes sunk before the purchase decision
Average satisfaction determines every additional purchase
after.commonError: Failing to transfer marginal comparison to an individual purchase.
after.feedback: The consumer continues while the next unit’s marginal benefit covers its marginal cost.
